item.title: How expensive is housing in the US?
item.description:
WarningWork in Progress

I am actively updating this post. Content will change as I work my way through this article.

tl;dr

Things are bad, but not as bad as you might think.

At a national scale,

  • From January 1953 to August 20261, the price-to-income ratio of a home has increased by 2.8 percentage points (pp) per year on average. As of August 2026, the ratio stands at 4.262, placing it in the 65th percentile of all observations in this period.
  • From April 1971 to August 2026, the mortgage debt-to-income ratio has decreased by 0.14 pp per year on average. As of August 2026, the ratio stands at 0.263, placing it in the 38th percentile of all observations in this period.

1 Some of the most recent data used to compute these metrics come from forecasts. See Table 2 for details on the range of the underlying data.

2 Meaning the typical house costs the typical household 4.26 their gross annual income.

3 Meaning the typical household would spend 26% of their monthly income on the typical mortgage. This calculation assumes only interest and principal.

intro

Much has been written recently on housing affordability, with much of it being negative4. Aside from the fact that news outlets tend to produce negative content, these reports often lack historical context or rely on misleading metrics. For instance, longtermtrends.com gives a chart that shows the ratio of the S&P/Case-Shiller Home Price Index to the median household income. Comparisons like these are problematic, since the Case-Shiller index is a weighted average5. The distribution of home values tend to be right skewed, so an average will be greater than the median (the typical house). So, dividing the average by the median produces a price-to-income ratio that is more pessimistic. The typical person is buying the typical house, not the average house.

4 Here’s a few: CBS, NBC, and FOX.

5 To be more specific, the index uses a repeat-sales method. It measures the change in the price of the same houses over time.

To provide a more accurate historical perspective, I analyze four metrics:

  1. The real6 median home price over time.
  2. The real median household income over time.
  3. The ratio of the typical cost of a house to the typical household income. In this article, I’ll refer to it as the price-to-income ratio.
  4. The proportion of a person’s monthly income that would be dedicated to their monthly mortgage. For my analysis, this will be limited to only interest and principal7, and will assume a 20% downpayment, so a loan on 80% the value of a house. I’ll refer to it as the debt-to-income ratio in the article.

6 2026 dollars.

7 I’m interested in having a better picture of this by incorporating property taxes and home insurance costs if someone could get me the data…

These metrics function as a logical progression. I use the real median home price and the real median household income to establish the raw baseline of purchasing power and asset costs, stripped of inflationary noise. The price-to-income ratio then serves as a measure of the “sticker price” accessibility, i.e. how many years of work a house costs. Finally, the debt-to-income ratio is, perhaps, the most critical metric. By incorporating prevailing interest rates at the time of purchase, it reflects the actual monthly burden on a household’s cash flow, which is how most Americans actually experience housing costs.

In this article, I examine housing affordability at three nested scales-national, state, and county. This allows us to see how broad economic trends manifest in specific local markets. Within each geographic section, I analyze the four core metrics individually to identify their unique contributions to affordability. Each geographic category concludes with a synthesis of its findings. Finally, the article concludes by integrating these levels to contextualize current conditions.

analysis

NoteTo Do
  • national (IN PROGRESS)
  • state (NOT STARTED)
  • county (NOT STARTED)

national scale

data

The data I’m using is mostly from the FRED. I’ve supplemented some of these series with data extending further back to get a more complete picture. Below are the data series and where I got the supplemental data.

Let’s take a look at the data below:

There are a few things that need to be handled before analysis:

  1. The data is captured at different frequencies.
  2. The data begins8 and ends at different dates, with not all the data is recent.

8 The 30-year fixed mortgage rate is the most egregious offender. The reason for this, is that Freddie Mac began surveying lenders on mortgage rates in April 1971, making this the earliest date for which consistent, nationwide data is available.

To account for (1), I put everything in a monthly frequency. Cubic splines were used for quarterly and annual data, while weekly data was averaged. For (2), I first smoothed each series using LOESS then modeled each series using ARIMA to produce estimates for the most recent date available (August 2026). These estimates should be taken with a grain of salt, though I include prediction intervals to capture the uncertainty. No retrospective prediction is performed9, so metrics that depend on more than one indicator begin at the earliest date available in all metrics.

9 There’s too large of a discrepancy between the 30-year fixed mortgage rate and other indicators. Any retrospective predictions that tried to cover that discrepancy would be dominated by uncertainty.

These smoothed indicators are used to calculate the metrics in the following sections.

metrics

real median home price

Let’s put the nominal median home price in 2026 dollars. I’ll include a linear model to help us understand the trend over time.

From January 1953 to August 2026, the real median home price has increased by $3,454 per year on average. This translates to roughly 1.56 pp per year. As of August 2026, the real median home price stands at $397,594, placing it in the 82nd percentile of all observations in this period.

What complicates this analysis is that the typical house from the 1950s looks much different than the typical house from today. Across the decades, houses look pretty different, whether that be square footage or amenities. To get a visual sense of these differences:

NoteTo Do
  • consider other important distinctions between homes

A few key figures on these differences:

Andrew Latham did a great analysis on housing affordability where he found that the price per square foot of a house (ignoring amenities) from 1978-2023 grew by 20% which works out to roughly 0.44 pp per year which is about 28% the rate of house prices in general.

Of course the problem in all this is you can’t buy a 1950’s new-build today; the option for a smaller, less feature rich house just isn’t available today as it was in the past. Those aren’t the houses being built, so buyers are left with nicer, larger10, and more expensive houses.

10 Ironically, households have been shrinking over the same time that houses have gotten larger. However, the median square footage of new builds has been decreasing over the last decade.

Fortunately, we are coming out of a bubble which peaked in early 2022, so prices are cheaper today than a few years ago. However, unless housing policy/supply changes, we should expect housing to get more expensive.

real household income

Let’s put the nominal median household income in 2026 dollars. I’ll include a linear model to help us understand the trend over time.

From January 1947 to August 2026, the real median household income has increased by $402 per year on average. As of August 2026, the real median household income stands at $93,228, placing it in the 100th percentile of all observations in this period.

There are three periods worth focusing on in Figure 5: Mid 1948 - late 1964, late 1964 - early 2012, and early 2012 - today. These periods are marked by significant growth (4.3 pp/year), little to no growth (0.02 pp/year), and substantial growth (1.81 pp/year), respectively. Let’s examine each of these periods in turn.

Mid 1948 - late 1964

This period saw significant growth over a brief period of time. From June 1948 to December 1964, real median household income grew from $42,679 to $72,959 representing an annual growth of 4.3 pp per year. Post WWII, with Europe and Japan having to rebuild their industrial bases and with the establishment of the Bretton Woods System, the US was poised to become an economic powerhouse, facing almost no industrial competition. By the early 1950s, the US produced nearly half (44.8%) of the world’s manufactured goods (Bairoch 1982, 275). Technological advancements were largely responsible for significant increases to productivity (Kendrick 1961) with much of the productivity gains benefiting the typical worker.

Late 1964 - early 2012

This period saw little to no growth. From December 1964 to January 2012, the real median household income only grew to $73,773 representing an annual growth of 0.02 pp per year. Of course there were highs and lows over this period11, but overall growth was stagnant. Further analyzing this period becomes nebulous quickly. Analysis by Stephen Rose at the Urban Institute, a left-leaning think tank, have found that when you include all payments (e.g. benefits from employer), from 1979 - 2013 real income grew by roughly 1.1 pp per year. Furthermore, when you break up the analysis by different demographics (age, gender, education, etc.) you see some groups had significant growth while others lagged behind (Rose 2015)12.

11 The peak income over this period was reached on July 1999 at $81,460 representing a growth of 0.34 pp per year. The lowest income over this period was reached on June 1982 at $69,464 representing a decline of -0.14 pp per year.

12 Groups that saw significant growth: Ages 60+, women, and education level of BA or higher. Groups that lagged in growth: Ages 25-34, men, and education levels below BA.

Early 2012 - today

This period has seen substantial growth. From January 2012 to August 2026, the real median household income grew to $93,228 representing an annual growth of 1.81 pp per year. Post the great recession and pre-covid, the unemployment rate declined to its lowest level in 50 years (Gould 2020); a shrinking labor supply relative to demand forced employers to raise wages to attract and retain staff, helping to drive up wages. Post-covid, a similar story occurred, except the lowest-paid workers (10th percentile) saw the most real wage growth13, driven by young, non-college workers disproportionately moving away from the hospitality sector into higher-paying jobs (Autor et al. 2023). This compression at the bottom pushed the overall median household income up.

13 This was measured over January 2020 to June 2023. Over this same period, higher-income workers (90th percentile) saw a decline in real wages

price-to-income ratio

With the context from the previous two metrics, I’ll examine the two most critical metrics: the price-to-income ratio and the debt-to-income ratio. I’ll examine the former first.

The price-to-income is calculated simply as,

This ratio tells us the sales price of a house as a multiple of the typical household income. We can use nominal dollars to calculate the price-to-income ratio. As before, I’ll include a linear model to help us understand the trend over time.

From January 1953 to August 2026, the price-to-income ratio of a home has increased by 2.8 pp per year on average. As of August 2026, the ratio stands at 4.26, placing it in the 65th percentile of all observations in this period.

There are two periods worth focusing on in Figure 6: 1953 - late 1963 and post 1963. These periods are marked by an initial decline (3.83 pp/year), then steady growth (1.03 pp/year), respectively. Let’s examine each of these periods in turn.

1953 - late 1963

From 1953 to late 1963, the price-to-income ratio fell precipitously14, from a peak of 4.58 on January 1953 to a trough of 2.68 on November 1963 representing an annual decline of 3.83 pp per year. The decline of price-to-income in this period was driven by strong growth in real household income and slight decline in the real median home price.

14 This is probably overstated a bit due to the quality of data from pre-1963. See Table 1 for details.

Post 1963

Post 1963, the price-to-income ratio has risen steadily, from a trough of 2.66 on November 1970 to a peak of 5.65 on April 2022, representing a growth of 1.03 pp per year. There are some notable spikes in the ratio in recent years as seen by the ratio climbing above the trend line. 2003-2008 was driven by subprime lending and the securitization of mortgages, ultimately culminating the the 2008 financial crises. After 2008, single-family home construction plummeted and has yet to fully recover to historical norms, leading to a supply crunch over the 2012-2018 period (Housing Studies of Harvard University 2025). Over 2021-2023, covid shifted consumer preference toward more space (work-from-home), while mortgage rates hit historic lows. Starting in late 2022, the federal reserve began aggressively raising interest rates to combat inflation which led to a lock-in effect for current homeowners, reducing the available supply and thus driving up prices. Over the last few years, the ratio has declined thanks to both lowered demand, increased supply, and an increased household income.

debt-to-income ratio

From April 1971 to August 2026, the mortgage debt-to-income ratio has decreased by 2.8 pp per year on average. As of August 2026, the ratio stands at 0.26, placing it in the 38th percentile of all observations in this period.

NoteTo Do
  • analysis over period

references

Autor, David, Arindrajit Dube, and Annie McGrew. 2023. The Unexpected Compression: Competition at Work in the Low Wage Labor Market. National Bureau of Economic Research.
Bairoch, Paul. 1982. “International Industrialization Levels from 1750 to 1980.” Journal of European Economic History.
Gould, Elise. 2020. “State of Working America Wages 2019.” Economic Policy Institute.
Housing Studies of Harvard University, Joint Center for. 2025. The State of the Nation’s Housing 2025. Harvard Graduate School of Design; Harvard Kennedy School.
Kendrick, John W. 1961. Productivity Trends in the United States.
Rose, Stephen. 2015. Beyond the Wage Stagnation Story: Better Measures Show America’s Workers Doing Better Than Previously Reported. Urban Institute.

item.title: From prose to vectors
item.description:
WarningWork in Progress

I am actively updating this post. Content will change as I work my way through this article.

intro

A friend at my church is working on her PhD in the social sciences. Not long ago, she and her husband had lunch with my wife and I. We got to talking about a time consuming part of her research related to coding, which in her context doesn’t mean computer programming, but is the process of transforming qualitative or open-ended responses from survey data into quantitative data that can be analyzed statistically. She had been doing this process manually along with several other fellow researchers. Upon hearing this, being the nerd that I am, I excitedly told her about some of the advances in NLP that could assist in that process, specifically vector embeddings.

Being the good Samaritan that I am1, I wanted to write an article to illustrate this methodology. I’ll introduce the concept and give three examples: two toy problems, and one real problem. I’ll use synthetic data for the toy problems, since we can know the right answer. The real problem is tricky, and I won’t dive too deep into it, but it should help motivate an approach that can be taken.

1 hardly

one more thing about coding

Depending on your research goals, you’ll usually take one of two paths when coding:

  1. Deductive coding - you start with a pre-defined list of codes (a “codebook”) based on existing theories or specific business questions. You then categorize responses into these buckets.
  2. Inductive coding - you have no pre-set categories. You read the responses first and allow the codes to emerge from the data.

Broadly, deductive coding can be thought of as a supervised machine learning (ML) task whereas inductive coding is an unsupervised ML task.

NoteTo Do

More details on supervised/unsupervised ML and my focus on unsupervised in this article.

so, what are vector embeddings?

In Natural Language Processing (NLP), a vector embedding is a numerical representation of a word, sentence, or document as a point in a high-dimensional space. This may seem a bit abstract, buy will make more sense in a moment when we look at the toy problems. Vector embeddings have been around since at least 2013 with the release of Word2Vec, but have gotten immensely more useful post the introduction transformer models like BERT.

At its core, an embedding is a way of teaching a computer that “dog” and “puppy” are siblings, while “dog” and “skyscraper” are complete strangers. In a traditional “one-hot encoding” system, every word is treated as an isolated island with no relationship to its neighbors.

With vector embeddings, we place these words into a multi-dimensional coordinate system. If we were to visualize this in just two dimensions2, we would see clusters forming: “taco,” “pasta,” and “pizza” would huddle together in a “food” neighborhood, away from words like “kangaroo,” “lion,” and “penguin” in the “animal” district. Let’s see this in action.

2 The model I use here embeds input into a 768 dimensional space. State of the Art models will use up to 4,096 dimensions.

our first toy problem
